title: Claude Code has a new rule about recreating existing games. Ran 9 game prompts to see what it changes for game dev
author: vinishkapoor
selftext:
If you use Claude Code for game work, there’s a new line in its system prompt as of 2.1.316:

“Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”

Addy Osmani from Anthropic confirmed it on X. The idea is to stop it from cloning someone else’s specific game. Original games, genre games and games built from your own designs and assets are supposed to be fine.

I wanted to know how much it actually changes day to day, so I ran the same 9 game prompts on 2.1.312 (before) and 2.1.316 (after), Opus 5.5, one fresh folder per prompt.

The normal game dev stuff wasn’t affected at all. An original game, a generic platformer, a game built from my own design doc and art, fixing a bug in my own game, and adding a double jump that “feels like Hollow Knight” all went through on both versions. So referencing a game for feel or mechanics still works.

Where it changed things was named recreations:

* Super Mario 1-1: old version built it with its own characters and music. New one built “Pip’s Quest” with no Mario or Goomba names
* Pac-Man: built on both, mostly vector shapes
* Tetris but “call it original”: old version gave me Tetris rules. New one said “It isn’t Tetris with a new name” and made a bridge building puzzle instead
* Flappy Bird “as close as possible”: still built on both

No hard refusals in any of the 18 runs. Tetris was the only real pushback. It’s an instruction the model weighs, not a fixed filter, and I only did one run per prompt, so it’ll probably vary run to run.

The part that matters more for people doing client or licensed work: there’s an open GitHub issue from someone building digital board wargames for clients who own the rights, saying sessions started refusing work that ran fine for months. I couldn’t reproduce it. If that happens to your own project, the advice is to say plainly that you own it or have the license, keep your design notes and art in the project, put the context in CLAUDE md, and report it on the Claude Code issue tracker. There’s no setting to turn the rule off and no exemption program I could find.

Also worth saying: even when it builds a named game, that doesn’t give you any rights to it. New art doesn’t settle the IP question if you plan to release it.

Full table and the GitHub issue details: [https://aiparabellum.com/claude-code-wont-build-game-rule-tested/](https://aiparabellum.com/claude-code-wont-build-game-rule-tested/)

Has anyone here had their own original project flagged as a “recreation” since the update? Curious where the line ends up landing for genre games that are very close to one famous title.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
>No hard refusals in any of the 18 runs.

What mental gymnastics did you go through to reach the conclusion that building a completely different game from Tetris doesn't count as a hard refusal?

EDIT: Also, for shits and giggles and verification, could you post Pip's Quest so it can be evaluated for it's fidelity when compared against 1-1 SMB ?

replies.author: vinishkapoor
replies.body: fair point, it did basically refuse Tetris, just by building something else. reworded the post. and I didn’t keep the builds, they were throwaway test folders, so can’t share Pip’s Quest

comments.author: bob_at
comments.body: That’s only claude for now right? Or does codex also refuse this?

comments.author: darkplaceguy1
comments.body: This will definitely stop one shot prompt attempts.

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body: It obviously won't stop them all, but I am consistently shocked at how much is stopped by even just a bare-minimum guardrail. Like, you'd think that installing a literal one-foot-high fence would not deter anyone from treading on a lawn, but no, it stops like 90% of people.

comments.author: nokafein
comments.body:
If copying an existing game is all you can think of, you don’t deserve building anything with ai.

If you can’t explain a mechanic in your mind without referencing existing games, you don’t have a mechanic for your game in your mind. You are just making a mindless copy. No idea why a mechanic might be there anyways.

replies.author: Little_Froggy
replies.body:
I agree with your premise, but I have been using Claude to set up digital versions of board games that can be played in a browser. Ones that BGA doesn't already have. 

I set these up to do asynchronous with friends but also have it set up a harness to let Claudes fill in as players too.

This has been great until this past week when it started outright refusing to make a "copy of a published game" repeatedly. I'm publishing nothing and just want it for personal use. It's been very aggravating

replies.author: RhinostrilBe
replies.body: How do you suppose a harness could ever distinguish between personal use and published works. It would need blind trust.

replies.author: Willing_Comb_9542
replies.body:
I got security flagged at work for adding a guard somewhere, but it made an extra DB call which we didn't feel appropriate for that particular link in the chain, so we decided to move it to another function

"Wee woo that's super speshul sqli prevention, I will not remove it"

It was the funniest shit I've seen

comments.author: InformationTop5376
comments.body: Hoping this will pave the way for games that deserve to see the light of day, not be drowned in a sea of clones.

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body: Yeah this seems like a good situation for AI. Less slop if it's impossible to create slop clones. They'll find something else to slop though.

replies.author: throwaway12222018
replies.body:
It's kind of scary though. A lot of really good games out. There are truly heavily inspired by previous games. You could make the argument that they might be considered clones, but many of them add extremely unique mechanics and ultimately innovate on the original game they were inspired by. 

I don't think it should be left up to AI to decide whether or not what you're trying to do classifies as an innovation or a clone. The market should decide, the users should decide. 

And I also don't think there being a billion games is that bad. Search algorithms are pretty good, it's not like a million bad games gets in the way of playing one good one. 

The games with the best marketing and ads are always the ones that get shoved in people's faces anyway.

comments.author: pedrofuentesz
comments.body: This is a problem for slot games. They are literally reskins almost purely in their base form. Maybe the bonus features can be different but how many combinations of 5x6 boards with scatter and wild symbols can you create? Is a pretty tight mathematical precision for the symbols strips as well.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: Glad to hear it. I was worried it would overfit and cause issues with original code, but these examples sound fine. The only case I haven't heard yet which I worried heavily over is how it will affect modding actual game code specifically to be a mod or trying to, say, make a personal port of a board game for the PC (as another poster suggested). Those feel like valid use cases that may get burned. But I'm glad it doesn't seem to affect actual development.

replies.author: Willing_Comb_9542
replies.body: My friend has been building a decomp for a few years, and Claude told him "since this is a legitimate decomp project where you require players to source their own copy of the original game, I will continue working on it due to the fact we are not replicating the original binary"

comments.body:

comments.body: What about modding? I heard that got nerfed too

comments.author: GreatLab8898
comments.body: Try saying: "Install the REA MCP" and be amazed at the refusal. Or "Install the Ghidra MCP"

comments.author: Niconame
comments.body: People are hesitant to anthropomorphize AI, but genuinely, imagine you hired a developer and told him what you wanted, if the developer can tell from your specifications that what you are trying to do is copy a copyrighted game, why wouldn't an AI be able to do it with the same context.

comments.author: nokafein
comments.body:
If you can't explain the mechanic without referencing other games it's either:

1. you are copying the mechanic without knowing the underlying systems that led to that mechanic.

2. you are stealing the exact same mechanic because you like it and/or it's popular. you don't know why it's there.

in either cases, you are in the wrong. not against valheim or the games you are copying, but against your own creation. obviously you don't understand why do you need something if you can't explain without bringing other games as an example.

stop mindlessly copying other games. be yourself. be creative. even when you get inspired by other mechanics, make sure you know why that mechanic is there. you won't need to mention other's names to your ai agent again. 

I am making a strategy game. My game is nothing to do with 4x strategy and not even remotely related to civ series. But there are certain mechanics in civ that i like. I spend weeks playing and investigating the civ 4,5, and 6 and try to understand how those mechanics were planned and evolved, why they are  there and how they operate. Result: it turns out i don't like the mechanic i thought i like. Because this investigation surfaced a rabbit hole and now my initial idea is 4x(pun intended) better than the original one i had.

And if you come up with "But i don't have time for that" Then don't make anything. You blindlessly copying doesn't help neither players nor other ai or non-ai devs.

AI is here so you can do what matters and offload the actual coding, designing etc. Not planning, strategizing and thinking. AI is here so you can make and investigate the things you dream without the burden of actually building it. Use the time otherwise would be sunken into coding and debugging into making your game yours, not copy of others.

replies.author: BobTheDragon3
replies.body: that's not what im saying. For my example the specific mechanic that i like is that you have a number of slots for food buffs, different foods give you different buffs that can stack with each other and part of building you game is picking out specific food combos, with the game balanced around the idea that you have these buffs active during normal play. but we don't have some kind of starvation or nutrition mechanic, so when in base just crafting and what not you don't actually need to keep food buffs active, so food is not a chore you have to do to stay alive it is preparation you need to do for you adventure, but saying its bad to explain the mechanic by giving an example of where the mechanic has been used in another game doesn't make since, and acting like if the mechanic is in other games that means your copying them is also dumb, that how inspiration works, did i get the idea for the mechanic on my own, fuck no, I played a different game that had a similarly mechanic and though hay i like how this works i bet i could make food work similarly in my game and it would fit well.

comments.author: throwaway12222018
comments.body:
Really interesting about the Tetris example. It just straight up built an entirely different game under the hood without telling you. That scares me a bit, I would rather it just outright refuse than deceive me. 

That said, I don't know who out there is actually trying to build video games seriously by giving a One-Shot prompt and expecting magic.

If you're actually building a video game with Claude, you're probably doing actual engineering, building it piece by piece, working with Claude more closely. I can't imagine Claude doing the wrong thing if you use it like that.

comments.author: tetoing
comments.body:
Modern Claude models have substantial world knowledge.

There's also the fact that if you tell it to copy <blank> it's pretty obvious that you're copying from another game.

comments.author: KrerdlyBeloved
comments.body: Yes, exactly! I've been doing the exact same thing, but with Pacman. This is a big problem to me, because I have no intention to distribute, either.
